==Problem==

Alicia had two containers. The first was <imath>\tfrac{5}{6}</imath> full of water and the second was empty. She poured all the water from the first container into the second container, at which point the second container was <imath>\tfrac{3}{4}</imath> full of water. What is the ratio of the volume of the first container to the volume of the second container?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } \frac{5}{8} \qquad \textbf{(B) } \frac{4}{5} \qquad \textbf{(C) } \frac{7}{8} \qquad \textbf{(D) } \frac{9}{10} \qquad \textbf{(E) } \frac{11}{12}</imath>

==Solution 1==

Let the first jar's volume be <imath>A</imath> and the second's be <imath>B</imath>. It is given that <imath>\frac{5}{6}A=\frac{3}{4}B</imath>. We find that <imath>\frac{A}{B}=\frac{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}{\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)}=\boxed{\textbf{(D) }\frac{9}{10}}.</imath> 

We already know that this is the ratio of the smaller to the larger volume because it is less than <imath>1.</imath>

==Solution 2==

An alternate solution is to substitute an arbitrary maximum volume for the first container - let's say <imath>72</imath>, so there was a volume of <imath>60</imath> in the first container, and then the second container also has a volume of <imath>60</imath>, so you get <imath>60 \cdot \frac{4}{3} = 80</imath>. Thus the answer is <imath>\frac{72}{80} = \boxed{\textbf{(D) }\frac{9}{10}}</imath>.
